{
"title": "A Single-domain Protein Catenane of Dihydrofolate Reductase",
"authors": "Jing Fang (Peking University); Tianzuo Li (Peking University); Jiyeon Lee (Pohang University of Science and Technology (POSTECH)); Dahye Lim (Pohang University of Science and Technology (POSTECH)); Lianjie Xu (Peking University); Yajie Liu (Peking University); Jongcheol Seo (Pohang University of Science and Technology (POSTECH)); Wen-Bin Zhang (Peking University)",
"field_subfield": "Protein engineering / synthetic biology (topological proteins)",
"type_of_paper": "Research article (design and synthesis of a novel single-domain protein catenane)",
"executive_summary": "Proteins are usually built from linear polypeptide chains, which limits their topological diversity, yet natural topological proteins suggest that unconventional topology can enhance stability. Artificial topological proteins have been made with 'assembly-reaction' synergy, but they typically contain multiple domains, complicating the study of topological effects. Ideally, a single-domain topological protein would show the most profound impact of topology. Here, the authors design and synthesize a single-domain protein catenane of dihydrofolate reductase (cat-DHFR), consisting of two mechanically interlocked polypeptide rings that fold synergistically. The design rewires connectivity between secondary motifs to introduce artificial entanglement, using the original DHFR fold itself as the entangling template, so no exogenous entangling motif is needed. Synthesis is achieved in cells via programmed streamlined post-translational processing using two pairs of mutually orthogonal split-intein ligation pairs, without additional in vitro reactions. The target P-2 molecule contains few exogenous motifs and is characterized by LC-MS, SDS-PAGE, protease cleavage, and ion mobility mass spectrometry. Compared to a linear control, cat-DHFR retains catalytic capability and shows enhanced stability against thermal or chemical denaturation due to conformational restriction. The authors conclude that linear proteins can be converted into concatenated single-domain counterparts with almost identical chemical composition, well-preserved function, and elevated stability. This represents a new horizon in protein science. The study demonstrates feasibility of the approach by converting a model enzyme, DHFR from Escherichia coli, into its single-domain catenane counterpart. DHFR catalyzes reduction of DHF to THF in the presence of NADPH. The authors show that chemical topology can be changed without collapsing the fold and can bring profound changes in properties. The work is notable because it eliminates the need for an exogenous entangling motif as a template, using spatially entangled relationships among secondary structures. The results support the hypothesis that single-domain topological proteins can be realized and that topology can enhance stability while largely preserving function. The study provides a general strategy for converting linear proteins into topological single-domain proteins, which could be extended to other domains and used for further engineering and evolution.",

summary.title: A Single-domain Protein Catenane of Dihydrofolate Reductase
summary.authors: Jing Fang (Peking University); Tianzuo Li (Peking University); Jiyeon Lee (Pohang University of Science and Technology (POSTECH)); Dahye Lim (Pohang University of Science and Technology (POSTECH)); Lianjie Xu (Peking University); Yajie Liu (Peking University); Jongcheol Seo (Pohang University of Science and Technology (POSTECH)); Wen-Bin Zhang (Peking University)
summary.type_of_paper: Research article (design and synthesis of a novel single-domain protein catenane)
summary.executive_summary: Proteins are usually built from linear polypeptide chains, which limits their topological diversity, yet natural topological proteins suggest that unconventional topology can enhance stability. Artificial topological proteins have been made with 'assembly-reaction' synergy, but they typically contain multiple domains, complicating the study of topological effects. Ideally, a single-domain topological protein would show the most profound impact of topology. Here, the authors design and synthesize a single-domain protein catenane of dihydrofolate reductase (cat-DHFR), consisting of two mechanically interlocked polypeptide rings that fold synergistically. The design rewires connectivity between secondary motifs to introduce artificial entanglement, using the original DHFR fold itself as the entangling template, so no exogenous entangling motif is needed. Synthesis is achieved in cells via programmed streamlined post-translational processing using two pairs of mutually orthogonal split-intein ligation pairs, without additional in vitro reactions. The target P-2 molecule contains few exogenous motifs and is characterized by LC-MS, SDS-PAGE, protease cleavage, and ion mobility mass spectrometry. Compared to a linear control, cat-DHFR retains catalytic capability and shows enhanced stability against thermal or chemical denaturation due to conformational restriction. The authors conclude that linear proteins can be converted into concatenated single-domain counterparts with almost identical chemical composition, well-preserved function, and elevated stability. This represents a new horizon in protein science. The study demonstrates feasibility of the approach by converting a model enzyme, DHFR from Escherichia coli, into its single-domain catenane counterpart. DHFR catalyzes reduction of DHF to THF in the presence of NADPH. The authors show that chemical topology can be changed without collapsing the fold and can bring profound changes in properties. The work is notable because it eliminates the need for an exogenous entangling motif as a template, using spatially entangled relationships among secondary structures. The results support the hypothesis that single-domain topological proteins can be realized and that topology can enhance stability while largely preserving function. The study provides a general strategy for converting linear proteins into topological single-domain proteins, which could be extended to other domains and used for further engineering and evolution.

Research Context
Proteins are typically linear, limiting topological diversity. Natural topological proteins suggest topology can enhance stability. Topology is now recognized as a dimension for protein engineering. Artificial topological proteins are made via assembly-reaction synergy.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether single-domain topological proteins can be made. The hypothesis is that single-domain topological proteins show the most profound topological impact. The hypothesis is that topology can enhance stability relative to linear counterparts. The predicted outcome is that topology can be changed without collapsing the fold. The predicted outcome is that function can be largely preserved.

Methodological Details
The model enzyme is DHFR from Escherichia coli. The wild-type DHFR structure is PDB 4KJJ. The design uses two mutually orthogonal split-intein ligation pairs. The split site is between residues 88 and 89. Ring I spans residues 1-88 and ring II spans residues 89-159. The split gives a GLN of +0.726 for the two segments. The final cat-DHFR has a GLN of +1.120. Ring I is circularly permutated to generate new termini between residues 23 and 24. The new loops are at least 16 residues long. The gene cassette contains two DHFR segments, two split-intein pairs, and a TEV site. The linear control is l-DHFR with extra amino acids at the termini. Genes are sub-cloned to pMCSG19 and pET21a vectors. The cells used are E.coli BL21(DE3) competent cells. Expression is at 16 o C for 20 h. Purification uses Ni-NTA affinity chromatography and size exclusion chromatography. The enzyme cofactor is NADPH. The substrate is DHF and the product is THF.

Procedures And Architectures
The design uses the Gaussian linking number matrix to identify the split position. The split traverses all unstructured loops. The design minimizes the number of split loops. The active site and adjacent regions are left intact. The gene cassette is designed for ring closure and topology proof. The split-intein pairs enable trace-less reconstitution and cyclization. The TEV site enables proof of topology by proteolytic digestion. The cells are transformed with the plasmids. Proteins are purified under native conditions. The activity is assayed by DHFR reduction with NADPH. The kinetic curves are monitored at 340 nm at 25 o C. The kinetic parameters are fitted by Michaelis curve and Hanes-Woolf plot. The binding affinity is measured by isothermal titration calorimetry. The topology is characterized by IMS and CID. The topology is confirmed by SDS-PAGE and LC-MS.

Key Results
l-DHFR shows a single band at ~22 kDa. cat-DHFR shows a major band at less than 20 kDa. cat-DHFR has faint bands at lower molecular weights. cat-DHFR elutes as a broader peak at a slightly larger retention volume. cat-DHFR has an accurate molecular weight in LC-MS. cat-DHFR remains folded but with reduced CD intensities. cat-DHFR has reduced positive peak at ~200 nm. cat-DHFR has reduced negative peak between 210 nm and 230 nm. cat-DHFR has positive ellipticity at ~290 nm. The same-side construct gives ~33% catenane form. The site between residues 23 and 24 is the most efficient. cat-DHFR has ~5 U/mg activity versus ~14 U/mg for l-DHFR. cat-DHFR retains ~87% activity in 5% DMSO versus ~74% for l-DHFR. cat-DHFR has a Km ~5-fold that of l-DHFR. cat-DHFR has a kcat ~38% that of l-DHFR. cat-DHFR has a catalytic efficiency reduced by an order of magnitude. cat-DHFR has a KD ~173-fold larger for DHF. cat-DHFR has a KD ~14-fold larger for NADPH. cat-DHFR has a KD ~3.6-fold larger for THF.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
cat-DHFR retains catalytic capability. cat-DHFR shows enhanced stability due to conformational restriction. The reduced activity is attributed to compromised affinity. The binding of NADPH enhances affinity toward DHF. The product THF can easily leave the enzyme. Mechanical interlocking enhances thermal resilience. The fold is a prerequisite for catenane formation. The topology reinforces the fold. The approach eliminates the need for an exogenous entangling motif. Linear proteins can be converted into concatenated single-domain counterparts. The results represent a new horizon in protein science.

Contradictions And Limitations
cat-DHFR has lower activity than l-DHFR. The reduced activity is attributed to compromised affinity. The reduced activity may be restored by directed evolution. The authors could not obtain a crystal structure. The crystallization failure may be due to unsatisfactory purity. The crystallization failure may be due to disordered linkers. The crystallization failure may be due to reduced binding affinity. The authors could not obtain crystals of sufficient quality. The authors had to resort to indirect characterization. The SEC peak is broad, suggesting a dynamic structure. The SEC peak is broader at a slightly larger retention volume. The same-side construct gives less catenane product. The linker length affects the yield. The catenated products could still be obtained with the shortest linker. The circular permutation may cause minor local disturbance. The overall structure is intact despite circular permutation. The authors could not fully characterize the topology. The authors could not obtain a crystal structure. The authors could not fully characterize the topology. The authors could not obtain a crystal structure.

Claims
A single-domain protein catenane of DHFR can be designed and synthesized in cells without additional in vitro reactions. The synthesis uses split-intein pairs. The synthesis uses the original DHFR fold as the template. The synthesis requires no additional in vitro reactions. The synthesis is accomplished in cells. The synthesis requires extensive optimization. The same-side construct gives less catenane product. The linker length affects the yield. The approach eliminates the need for an exogenous entangling motif. The approach can be extended to other domains. The approach provides a new horizon in protein science.
cat-DHFR retains catalytic capability and shows enhanced stability relative to the linear control. cat-DHFR retains catalytic capability. cat-DHFR shows enhanced stability. cat-DHFR retains ~87% activity in 5% DMSO. cat-DHFR retains ~74% activity for l-DHFR. cat-DHFR has lower activity than l-DHFR. cat-DHFR has a Km ~5-fold that of l-DHFR. cat-DHFR has a kcat ~38% that of l-DHFR. cat-DHFR has a KD ~173-fold larger for DHF. Topology can enhance stability while largely preserving function. The reduced activity may be restored by directed evolution. The results represent a new horizon in protein science.

Data And Code Availability

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the design and synthesis of a single-domain protein catenane of DHFR. 2. The strongest evidence is the retention of catalytic capability and enhanced stability. 3. The future path is the extension of the approach to other domains and directed evolution.
